resources.title: North American porcupine
resources.description: Identify the north american porcupine (Erethizon dorsatum), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: North American porcupine (Erethizon dorsatum): Dark brown to black overall, stout, slow, lumbering form. Dorsal guard hairs and quills banded with yellow; quills run head to tail on the back. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Central Alaska east to southern Hudson Bay and Labrador; south to the northeastern US in the east and to central Texas, northern Mexico and southern California in the west.

rangeSummary.value: Central Alaska east to southern Hudson Bay and Labrador; south to the northeastern US in the east and to central Texas, northern Mexico and southern California in the west.

identification.text: Dark brown to black overall, stout, slow, lumbering form.
Dorsal guard hairs and quills banded with yellow; quills run head to tail on the back.
Black line along middle of tail and lower back, with white-fringed quills, visible from about three months of age.
Length 600-900 mm; 5-14 kg; about 30,000 barbed quills, about 75 mm long.

habitat.text: Prefers coniferous and mixed forest; also riparian zones, grasslands, shrublands and some deserts. Winter dens in rock outcrops, hollow trees or logs, or outbuildings.

behavior.text: Mainly nocturnal but frequently seen by day
Winter food: inner bark of trees and evergreen needles; buds in spring; roots, leaves, berries, fruit and seeds in summer
Threat display: chatters teeth, releases an odour and shows the white-on-black marking

resources.title: American ermine
resources.description: Identify the american ermine (Mustela richardsonii), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: American ermine (Mustela richardsonii): Typical weasel form: long body, short legs, triangular head, round ears, long whiskers. Summer: chocolate-brown back with yellowish-white belly. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Across Canada and south through most of the northern US to central California, northern Arizona, northern New Mexico, Iowa, the Great Lakes region, Pennsylvania and northern Virginia. Most of Alaska now refers to M. erminea.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe: split from Mustela erminea by Colella et al. (2021) into M. erminea, M. richardsonii and M. haidarum. The ADW page read describes the pre-split M. erminea.
Split from Mustela erminea (2021); most of Canada and the contiguous US

rangeSummary.value: Across Canada and south through most of the northern US to central California, northern Arizona, northern New Mexico, Iowa, the Great Lakes region, Pennsylvania and northern Virginia. Most of Alaska now refers to M. erminea.

identification.text: Typical weasel form: long body, short legs, triangular head, round ears, long whiskers.
Summer: chocolate-brown back with yellowish-white belly.
Winter: white coat in northern animals, with a black tail tip.
Tail about 35% of body length; males roughly twice the mass of females (ADW page for pre-split M. erminea).
Compared with the beringian ermine: Same look; Alaska and western Yukon to Arctic Canada animals are M. erminea per NatureServe.
Compared with the least weasel: Much smaller with no black tail tip.
Compared with the long-tailed weasel: Larger, with a tail about half the body length.

habitat.text: Wooded areas with thick understory near watercourses; adapted to a wide variety of habitats and rarely in heavily forested regions.

behavior.text: Mainly nocturnal but frequently seen by day
Eats mainly small mammals, occasionally other small vertebrates and insects
In winter in southern Ontario, usually stayed beneath the snow surface
Dens in hollow logs, under stumps, roots, brush piles or rocks

resources.title: Ermine
resources.description: Identify the ermine (Mustela erminea), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Ermine (Mustela erminea): Typical weasel form: long body, short legs, triangular head, slightly protruding round ears. White winter coat with a black tail tip. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Much of Eurasia; in North America, Alaska and western Yukon to most of Arctic Canada and east to Greenland per NatureServe. The widespread North American animal is now M. richardsonii.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe lists this as the Beringian ermine after the 2021 split (Colella et al.); mainland North American animals are M. richardsonii.
After the 2021 split, the Beringian species: Alaska, Yukon and the northwest

rangeSummary.value: Much of Eurasia; in North America, Alaska and western Yukon to most of Arctic Canada and east to Greenland per NatureServe. The widespread North American animal is now M. richardsonii.

identification.text: Typical weasel form: long body, short legs, triangular head, slightly protruding round ears.
White winter coat with a black tail tip.
Summer: chocolate-brown back, yellowish-white underside up to the upper lip.
Body 170-330 mm; tail about 35% of body length; males about twice the mass of females.
Compared with the american ermine: Same appearance; separated by range, with M. richardsonii across most of Canada and the northern US.

habitat.text: Riparian woodlands, marshes, shrubby fencerows and open areas adjacent to forest or shrub borders.

behavior.text: Uses riparian woodlands, marshes, fencerows and open areas next to forest
Climbs trees and swims well; dens in tree roots, hollow logs, stone walls and rodent burrows

resources.title: Long-tailed weasel
resources.description: Identify the long-tailed weasel (Neogale frenata), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Long-tailed weasel (Neogale frenata): Long slender body, small narrow head, long whiskers, short legs. Cinnamon-brown above, white underparts with a yellow tinge. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern Canada, nearly all of the contiguous US (excluding the southwestern deserts), south to Venezuela and Bolivia.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe moved this species from Mustela to Neogale (Patterson et al. 2021); ADW still uses Mustela frenata.

rangeSummary.value: Southern Canada, nearly all of the contiguous US (excluding the southwestern deserts), south to Venezuela and Bolivia.

identification.text: Long slender body, small narrow head, long whiskers, short legs.
Cinnamon-brown above, white underparts with a yellow tinge.
Long bushy tail about 50% of body length.
Body 330-420 mm in males, 280-350 mm in females; northern animals turn white in winter, southern ones stay brown.
Compared with the least weasel: Far smaller with a short tail and no black tip in winter.
Compared with the american ermine: Shorter tail relative to body.

habitat.text: A wide variety of habitats, usually near water: brushland, open woodland, field edges, riparian grassland, swamps and marshes; not desert or thick forest.

behavior.text: Primarily nocturnal but frequently seen by day
Eats mainly small mammals, occasionally birds, other small vertebrates and insects
Dens in abandoned burrows, rock crevices, brush piles, stump hollows or among tree roots
Molts in spring and fall, timed by day length

resources.title: Least weasel
resources.description: Identify the least weasel (Mustela nivalis), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Least weasel (Mustela nivalis): Smallest carnivore in the family: long tubular body, short tail under a quarter of head-body length. Winter coat pure white in northern animals, but never a black tail tip. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Circumboreal. Most of Canada and Alaska, south to British Columbia, Montana, Wyoming, Oklahoma, Missouri, Ohio, Virginia and along the Appalachians; range has expanded south in the Great Plains since the mid-1960s.

rangeSummary.value: Circumboreal. Most of Canada and Alaska, south to British Columbia, Montana, Wyoming, Oklahoma, Missouri, Ohio, Virginia and along the Appalachians; range has expanded south in the Great Plains since the mid-1960s.

identification.text: Smallest carnivore in the family: long tubular body, short tail under a quarter of head-body length.
Winter coat pure white in northern animals, but never a black tail tip.
Summer: rusty chocolate-brown back, white belly.
North American animals average about 45 g and about 190 mm including tail.
Compared with the ermine / stoat: Larger with a black tail tip in winter.
Compared with the long-tailed weasel: Larger, with a long tail and black tip.

habitat.text: Open forests, farmland, grassy fields and meadows, riparian woodland, hedgerows, alpine meadows, scrub, prairies and coastal dunes; generally avoids deep dense forest.

behavior.text: Active day or night through the year
Specialist on small mammals, especially voles, lemmings and mice; also other small vertebrates, insects or worms when rodents are scarce
Uses abandoned burrows of prey; hunts in subnivean tunnels
Basically solitary outside breeding

resources.title: Western spotted skunk
resources.description: Identify the western spotted skunk (Spilogale gracilis), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Western spotted skunk (Spilogale gracilis): Small and slender, black with white spots on the forehead and in front of each ear. Stripes: dorsolateral pair from the back of the head, a lateral pair joining the ear spots, and a ventrolateral pair; they end at mid-body. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Much of the western United States, including the Channel Islands of California, and the Baja Peninsula.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe: split by McDonough et al. (2022) into western spotted skunk (S. gracilis) and desert spotted skunk (S. leucoparia).

rangeSummary.value: Much of the western United States, including the Channel Islands of California, and the Baja Peninsula.

identification.text: Small and slender, black with white spots on the forehead and in front of each ear.
Stripes: dorsolateral pair from the back of the head, a lateral pair joining the ear spots, and a ventrolateral pair; they end at mid-body.
Rear body has two interrupted white bands, a white rump spot each side and two at the tail base.
Underside of tail white for nearly half its length, tip extensively white.
Males about 423 mm and 565 g; females about 360 mm and 368 g.
Compared with the eastern spotted skunk: Looks similar but with less extensive white.

habitat.text: Brushy canyons, rocky outcrops and canyon walls; rocky bluffs and brush-bordered canyon stream beds; sometimes nests in rock fences or attics.

behavior.text: More nocturnal than the striped skunk and rarely seen by day; active year round
Eats insects, rodents, small birds, possibly eggs, reptiles, amphibians, fruit and berries
Dens in rocks, burrows, hollow logs, brush piles and under buildings
Essentially solitary

resources.title: Eastern spotted skunk
resources.description: Identify the eastern spotted skunk (Spilogale putorius), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Eastern spotted skunk (Spilogale putorius): Small, weasel-like skunk with a small white spot on the forehead and one in front of each ear. Six distinct white stripes on the front of the body; rear body has two interrupted white bands. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: NatureServe places S. putorius east of the Mississippi River, from the Florida peninsula north to at least Pennsylvania.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe (McDonough et al. 2022) splits the eastern spotted skunk into S. putorius (Alleghanian, east of the Mississippi) and S. interrupta (plains spotted skunk); the ADW page predates the split.
South Carolina's furbearer season names spotted skunk, which there can only be this species

rangeSummary.value: NatureServe places S. putorius east of the Mississippi River, from the Florida peninsula north to at least Pennsylvania.

identification.text: Small, weasel-like skunk with a small white spot on the forehead and one in front of each ear.
Six distinct white stripes on the front of the body; rear body has two interrupted white bands.
White spot each side of the rump and two at the tail base.
Front claws sharp, recurved and more than twice as long as hind claws.
Compared with the western spotted skunk: White areas more extensive on the western species.

habitat.text: Prefers forested areas or habitats with significant cover; ADW also gives wooded areas, tall-grass prairie and rocky habitats.

behavior.text: Mostly nocturnal; mostly inactive in winter
Opportunistic omnivore: small mammals, grubs and insects, corn, grapes, berries
Dens in abandoned burrows, brush piles, hollow logs or trees, rock crevices and under buildings

resources.title: American hog-nosed skunk
resources.description: Identify the american hog-nosed skunk (Conepatus leuconotus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: American hog-nosed skunk (Conepatus leuconotus): Single white stripe from the top of the head, wedge-shaped at the start, to the tail tip; some northwestern animals have more white. Large naked snout resembling a hog's; small eyes and nose relative to the snout. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southwestern US south to northern Nicaragua. In the US: southeastern Colorado, extreme northwestern Oklahoma, Arizona, New Mexico and western Texas.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe: C. leuconotus and C. mesoleucus were formerly separate species; Wozencraft (2005) included mesoleucus in C. leuconotus.
Texas says only "skunk"

rangeSummary.value: Southwestern US south to northern Nicaragua. In the US: southeastern Colorado, extreme northwestern Oklahoma, Arizona, New Mexico and western Texas.

identification.text: Single white stripe from the top of the head, wedge-shaped at the start, to the tail tip; some northwestern animals have more white.
Large naked snout resembling a hog's; small eyes and nose relative to the snout.
Short coarse fur; tail mostly white above.
Stocky legs; front claws larger for digging.
Males average about 577 mm total length, females about 542 mm.

habitat.text: Woodlands, grasslands, deserts, brushy areas and rocky canyons; most common in very rocky mountainous terrain.

behavior.text: Mostly nocturnal, sometimes active by day especially in winter; active year round
Feeds mainly on insects, especially larvae; digs and roots with snout and long claws, overturning rocks and logs
Dens in rock crevices, hollow logs, burrows, caves, mine shafts, woodrat houses or under buildings

resources.title: Ringtail
resources.description: Identify the ringtail (Bassariscus astutus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Ringtail (Bassariscus astutus): Long bushy tail ringed black and white, roughly as long as the head and body. Buffy body with dark brown wash and pale buff underparts. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Western North America north to southern Oregon, northern Nevada, northern Utah, southern Wyoming and Colorado, south through California, Arizona, New Mexico and Texas into Mexico; old records from Kansas.

rangeSummary.value: Western North America north to southern Oregon, northern Nevada, northern Utah, southern Wyoming and Colorado, south through California, Arizona, New Mexico and Texas into Mexico; old records from Kansas.

identification.text: Long bushy tail ringed black and white, roughly as long as the head and body.
Buffy body with dark brown wash and pale buff underparts.
Black or dark brown eye rings set in buffy patches.
Cat-like body, fox-like face, large oval ears, semi-retractable claws.
Head and body 305-420 mm, 824-1,338 g.
Compared with the raccoon: ADW notes a ringed tail much like a raccoon's; ringtail is far slimmer, cat-like, with a much longer tail.

habitat.text: Rocky areas with cliffs, crevices, canyons or talus in desert scrub, chaparral, oak and pinyon-juniper woodland and montane conifer forest, usually within 0.5 mile of water.

behavior.text: Mainly nocturnal, also at dusk and dawn; active year round
Omnivorous but prefers animal matter: arthropods, small mammals, fruit, birds, reptiles, amphibians
Calls include an explosive bark and a piercing scream
Secretive; occurs singly or in pairs; changes dens often

resources.title: Swift fox
resources.description: Identify the swift fox (Vulpes velox), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Swift fox (Vulpes velox): Small fox with a black-tipped tail and black patches on either side of the snout. Winter coat dark buffy gray above, orange-tan on sides, legs and underside of tail; summer coat shorter and more reddish. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Historically the central plains from southern Alberta and Saskatchewan to northern Texas, including southern Manitoba; present range is much restricted, nearly continuous from Wyoming south through eastern Colorado, western Kansas, the Oklahoma Panhandle and eastern New Mexico.

taxonomicNotes.text: Once treated as the same species as the kit fox; NatureServe treats V. macrotis as separate.

rangeSummary.value: Historically the central plains from southern Alberta and Saskatchewan to northern Texas, including southern Manitoba; present range is much restricted, nearly continuous from Wyoming south through eastern Colorado, western Kansas, the Oklahoma Panhandle and eastern New Mexico.

identification.text: Small fox with a black-tipped tail and black patches on either side of the snout.
Winter coat dark buffy gray above, orange-tan on sides, legs and underside of tail; summer coat shorter and more reddish.
Throat, chest, belly and inside of ears creamy white.
Head-body 38-53 cm, tail 23-35 cm, 1.8-3.0 kg.
Differs from kit fox in smaller ears, broader snout and shorter tail.
Compared with the kit fox: Larger ears, narrower snout, longer tail; more arid southwestern range.

habitat.text: Open prairie and arid plains, mainly shortgrass prairie; often digs dens in sandy soil, along fences or in plowed fields.

behavior.text: Primarily nocturnal; may rest in the sun outside the burrow by day
Dens in burrows it digs or takes over from other mammals
Opportunistic diet: jackrabbits, cottontails, ground squirrels, mice, birds, invertebrates, grasses, berries; caches food under snow in winter

resources.title: Kit fox
resources.description: Identify the kit fox (Vulpes macrotis), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Kit fox (Vulpes macrotis): Smallest canid in North America, 1.6-2.7 kg. Exceptionally large ears (71-95 mm) set close together. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southeastern Oregon, Nevada, Utah, western Colorado, southern California, Arizona, New Mexico and western Texas, south to central Mexico.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe treats V. macrotis as separate from V. velox.

rangeSummary.value: Southeastern Oregon, Nevada, Utah, western Colorado, southern California, Arizona, New Mexico and western Texas, south to central Mexico.

identification.text: Smallest canid in North America, 1.6-2.7 kg.
Exceptionally large ears (71-95 mm) set close together.
Yellowish to gray coat with a darker back and light underside and inner ears.
Distinct dark patches on each side of the nose and at the tail tip.
Compared with the swift fox: Smaller ears, broader snout, shorter tail; Great Plains range.

habitat.text: Open desert, shrubby or shrub-grass habitat, at 400-1,900 m; also chaparral, valley grassland and some agricultural and urban areas.

behavior.text: Basically nocturnal
Spends most of its time in dens, which it digs or takes over from prairie dogs, other rodents and badgers
Barks at perceived threats; uses a hacking growl with other foxes
Main prey is the most abundant nocturnal rodent or lagomorph locally

conservationStatus.text: San Joaquin kit fox (Vulpes macrotis mutica), wherever found: listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Act since 1967-03-11.

resources.title: Pacific marten
resources.description: Identify the pacific marten (Martes caurina), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Pacific marten (Martes caurina). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Much of the western US and part of southwestern Canada, including California, Nevada, Oregon, Washington, Utah, Colorado, New Mexico, Idaho, Montana, South Dakota, Alaska (Kuiu and Admiralty islands) and British Columbia.

taxonomicNotes.text: Recognized by NatureServe as separate from the American marten (M. americana). No field marks were sourced: ADW has no page under this name.

rangeSummary.value: Much of the western US and part of southwestern Canada, including California, Nevada, Oregon, Washington, Utah, Colorado, New Mexico, Idaho, Montana, South Dakota, Alaska (Kuiu and Admiralty islands) and British Columbia.

identification.text: Compared with the american marten: Separate species; Alaska, British Columbia, Idaho and Montana have both. NatureServe cites Dawson and Cook (2012).

habitat.text: Dense deciduous, mixed or especially coniferous forest, upland and lowland; may use rocky alpine areas; in winter in the central Rockies mainly old-growth forest.

behavior.text: Basically solitary; densities of about 1-2 martens per sq km recorded in early fall
Activity peaks at dusk and dawn in summer and is frequent by day in winter; foraging nocturnal in winter and diurnal in summer in the Sierra Nevada
Diet mostly small mammals, birds, insects and carrion; berries in season; hunts prey under the snow
Rests in tree cavities, stumps, squirrel nests, rock piles, burrows and snow cavities

conservationStatus.text: The pacific marten, coastal dps, wherever found: listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act since 2020-11-09.

resources.title: White-nosed coati
resources.description: Identify the white-nosed coati (Nasua narica), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: White-nosed coati (Nasua narica): Body length 80-130 cm, over half of it tail. Grayish-brown coat with silver grizzling; long pointed flexible snout. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Central Arizona, southwestern New Mexico and southern Texas south through Mexico and Central America; occurrences farther north in Arizona/New Mexico likely wanderers or released captives. Texas status uncertain.

taxonomicNotes.text: Arizona sets a season of one per calendar year under a hunting licence

rangeSummary.value: Central Arizona, southwestern New Mexico and southern Texas south through Mexico and Central America; occurrences farther north in Arizona/New Mexico likely wanderers or released captives. Texas status uncertain.

identification.text: Body length 80-130 cm, over half of it tail.
Grayish-brown coat with silver grizzling; long pointed flexible snout.
White band near the snout tip, white spots above and below each eye and on each cheek.
Long tapering tail with black rings, held erect when walking.
Black feet, forefeet with bent claws.
Compared with the ringtail: Much smaller, cat-like, with a short muzzle and a black-and-white ringed tail.

habitat.text: Broken tropical forest, pine forest, mesquite grassland and oak scrub; in the southwestern US, canyons, usually near water.

behavior.text: Primarily diurnal, some night activity; most active in morning and evening
Omnivorous; prefers fruit and berries; forages on the ground and in trees
Groups of a dozen or more (mothers and young) travel together; males are solitary most of the year

resources.title: Black-tailed prairie dog
resources.description: Identify the black-tailed prairie dog (Cynomys ludovicianus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Black-tailed prairie dog (Cynomys ludovicianus): Largest Cynomys; 700-1,500 g, 28-33 cm nose to rump, tail 7-10 cm. Dark cinnamon back and upper sides, buff underside. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: In Canada, limited to the Frenchman River Valley in southeastern Saskatchewan. In the US from eastern and central Montana and western North Dakota south to Texas and eastern New Mexico; extirpated from Arizona by the 1960s and since reintroduced.

commonNames.value: Chien de prairie à queue noire

rangeSummary.value: In Canada, limited to the Frenchman River Valley in southeastern Saskatchewan. In the US from eastern and central Montana and western North Dakota south to Texas and eastern New Mexico; extirpated from Arizona by the 1960s and since reintroduced.

identification.text: Largest Cynomys; 700-1,500 g, 28-33 cm nose to rump, tail 7-10 cm.
Dark cinnamon back and upper sides, buff underside.
Distal third of tail black or dark brown.
Small limbs, tail and ears.
Molts twice a year.

habitat.text: Dry, flat or gently sloping open grassland with short sparse vegetation, including overgrazed pasture; most abundant in mixed-grass and short-grass associations.

behavior.text: Active by day; rests in burrows in the hottest part of the day
Colonial, with 12 distinct calls including the 'jump-yip'
Mainly grasses and herbs; may reduce activity in winter (no torpor observed in a Colorado study)

resources.title: White-tailed prairie dog
resources.description: Identify the white-tailed prairie dog (Cynomys leucurus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: White-tailed prairie dog (Cynomys leucurus): Gray to yellowish-brown upper body with dark cheek patches / dark patches above and below each eye. Whitish to grayish tip on the short tail. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: From the Bighorn Basin in southern Montana across central and southwestern Wyoming into western and north-central Colorado and eastern Utah.

taxonomicNotes.text: Cynomys parvidens (Utah prairie dog) has been regarded by some authors as a subspecies; NatureServe cites Thorington and Hoffmann (2005) recognizing it as separate.

rangeSummary.value: From the Bighorn Basin in southern Montana across central and southwestern Wyoming into western and north-central Colorado and eastern Utah.

identification.text: Gray to yellowish-brown upper body with dark cheek patches / dark patches above and below each eye.
Whitish to grayish tip on the short tail.
Head and body 342-399 mm in males, 315-375 mm in females.
Usually at higher elevation than black-tailed prairie dogs.
Compared with the black-tailed prairie dog: Black-tipped tail and a lower-elevation, grassland habitat.

habitat.text: Open shrublands, semidesert grasslands and open valleys at 5,000-10,000 ft; sage is important cover.

behavior.text: Loosely colonial; alarm 'repetitious bark', 'laughing bark' for group cohesion, snarl and growl
Feeds mainly on forbs and grasses
Hibernates; emerges from late February-March, males 2-3 weeks before females; by late August all adults are inactive
Morning and late-afternoon activity in summer

resources.title: Gunnison's prairie dog
resources.description: Identify the gunnison's prairie dog (Cynomys gunnisoni), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Gunnison's prairie dog (Cynomys gunnisoni): Total length 309-373 mm; tail 39-68 mm, much shorter than other prairie dogs. Yellowish-buff coat mixed with blackish hairs; darker top of head, cheeks and eyebrows. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Central Colorado to central Arizona, including part of southeastern Utah and much of northwestern New Mexico.

rangeSummary.value: Central Colorado to central Arizona, including part of southeastern Utah and much of northwestern New Mexico.

identification.text: Total length 309-373 mm; tail 39-68 mm, much shorter than other prairie dogs.
Yellowish-buff coat mixed with blackish hairs; darker top of head, cheeks and eyebrows.
Tail base matches the back, distal half grayish with grayish-white hairs at the tip.
Compared with the white-tailed prairie dog: Pure white distal tail hairs versus grayish-white on Gunnison's.

habitat.text: Gently sloping grasslands and semi-desert and montane shrublands at 4,600-12,000 ft.

behavior.text: Colonies often small, under 50-100 animals, in territories of one adult male, one or more females and young
Most activity early morning and late afternoon in spring and summer
Inactive periods lasting months in winter; hibernation in some parts
Diet of grasses, forbs, sedges and shrubs

resources.title: Richardson's ground squirrel
resources.description: Identify the richardson's ground squirrel (Urocitellus richardsonii), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Richardson's ground squirrel (Urocitellus richardsonii): Stout body with short dense fur. Dorsum light pinkish or cinnamon buff with a dappled rear; countershaded lighter belly. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Northern Great Plains: southern Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, Montana, North Dakota, northeastern South Dakota, western Minnesota and northwestern Iowa.

taxonomicNotes.text: Now Urocitellus; ADW uses the older Spermophilus. NatureServe: ground squirrels formerly in Spermophilus are split into 8 genera (Helgen et al. 2009).

rangeSummary.value: Northern Great Plains: southern Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, Montana, North Dakota, northeastern South Dakota, western Minnesota and northwestern Iowa.

identification.text: Stout body with short dense fur.
Dorsum light pinkish or cinnamon buff with a dappled rear; countershaded lighter belly.
Darker cinnamon buff on front of forelegs, neck and sides of head; light buff eye ring.
Tail black above, cinnamon or clay below, edged pinkish buff.

habitat.text: Grasslands, rolling hills, fields and croplands; prefers gravelly or sandy soil and short grass around burrow entrances.

behavior.text: Hibernates, entering late August-October and emerging by late March or April
Activity peaks about 2 h after dawn, 10 am-2 pm and 4 pm to sunset; stays in the burrow in extreme heat or rain
Multi-syllable alarm calls vary with predator type
Eats herbaceous plants in spring, seeds and fruit in late summer and fall; stores seeds in burrows; loose colonies

resources.title: Columbian ground squirrel

resources.title: Nine-banded armadillo
resources.description: Identify the nine-banded armadillo (Dasypus novemcinctus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Nine-banded armadillo (Dasypus novemcinctus): Bony armour of rectangular or pentagonal plates in three sections; usually 9 bands, range 8-11. Unarmoured yellowish underside. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: South and Central America into the southern US, expanding north since the 1800s to Missouri and Illinois.

rangeSummary.value: South and Central America into the southern US, expanding north since the 1800s to Missouri and Illinois.

identification.text: Bony armour of rectangular or pentagonal plates in three sections; usually 9 bands, range 8-11.
Unarmoured yellowish underside.
About 0.75 m body plus 0.3 m tail; 3.6-7.7 kg.

habitat.text: Forest and scrub-brush with adequate water and at least 38 cm annual rainfall.

behavior.text: Mainly nocturnal or crepuscular; forages earlier on cold or cloudy days
Solitary except when mating; does not hibernate
Digs burrows up to 5 m long, up to 12 dens
Over 90% of diet is animal matter (beetles, termites, ants) found by smell

resources.title: Blackbuck
resources.description: Identify the blackbuck (Antilope cervicapra), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Blackbuck (Antilope cervicapra): Males dark brown above, white underparts, white eye patches; only males have spiral horns (50-61 cm, about 4 turns). Females yellowish where males are dark. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Native to India and Pakistan. The ADW page does not describe North American introduced populations.

rangeSummary.value: Native to India and Pakistan. The ADW page does not describe North American introduced populations.

identification.text: Males dark brown above, white underparts, white eye patches; only males have spiral horns (50-61 cm, about 4 turns).
Females yellowish where males are dark.
73.7-83.8 cm at shoulder; 32-43 kg.

habitat.text: Open woodland, semi-desert, thorn forest and dry deciduous forest near grassland.

behavior.text: Gregarious herds of 5-50 led by a single male
Shy and wary, relies on vision
Active early morning and late afternoon in hot seasons
Can hold about 40 mph for long distances

resources.title: Red deer
resources.description: Identify the red deer (Cervus elaphus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Red deer (Cervus elaphus): Dark brown in winter, tan in summer, with buff rump patch. Males carry large antlers and a dark neck-to-chest mane; 178-497 kg. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Formerly across the Northern Hemisphere; in North America now largely western. Introduced to Ireland, Argentina, Chile, Australia and New Zealand.

taxonomicNotes.text: ADW treats elk/wapiti and red deer as one species, Cervus elaphus, with regional variation; North Ground's separate red-deer record may need a scope note.
Distinct from elk, Cervus canadensis

rangeSummary.value: Formerly across the Northern Hemisphere; in North America now largely western. Introduced to Ireland, Argentina, Chile, Australia and New Zealand.

identification.text: Dark brown in winter, tan in summer, with buff rump patch.
Males carry large antlers and a dark neck-to-chest mane; 178-497 kg.
Females smaller, 171-292 kg.
0.75-1.5 m at shoulder.
Compared with the white-tailed deer: Occupies similar habitat but is much smaller (source only notes association).

habitat.text: Open woodland avoiding dense forest: conifer swamps, clearcuts, aspen-hardwood; sea level to 3,000 m.

behavior.text: Herds up to 400; males hold harems in the fall rut (late Sept-early Oct) and bugle
Browses early morning and evening; inactive by day

resources.title: Gemsbok
resources.description: Identify the gemsbok (Oryx gazella), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Gemsbok (Oryx gazella): Grey/tan body, white lower legs and belly. Black face markings extending down from horn bases; stripe along spine. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Native to southern Africa; successfully introduced to the southwestern US and Mexico.

rangeSummary.value: Native to southern Africa; successfully introduced to the southwestern US and Mexico.

identification.text: Grey/tan body, white lower legs and belly.
Black face markings extending down from horn bases; stripe along spine.
Slightly curved horns 60-150 cm; 115-125 cm at shoulder.
Males 180-240 kg, females 180-225 kg.

habitat.text: Stony plains, dunes, rocky hills and arid country.

behavior.text: Nomadic and gregarious, groups averaging 14; males often solitary and territorial
Crepuscular
Grazes, browses in drought, digs up to 1 m for tubers and roots

resources.title: Persian ibex
resources.description: Identify the persian ibex (Capra aegagrus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Persian ibex (Capra aegagrus): About 30 in (76 cm) at the shoulder, hindquarters noticeably higher than the front on flat ground. Mature males up to about 110 lb, females up to about 60 lb; both sexes grow horns (female horns average up to 15 in), male scimitar-shaped horns can exceed 50 in. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Native from Turkey and the Caucasus east to Iran, Turkmenistan, Afghanistan and Pakistan. In North America, introduced to the Florida Mountains near Deming, New Mexico in 1970.

taxonomicNotes.text: NM Department of Wildlife calls it Persian ibex (bezoar goat, Persian wild goat); Wikipedia treats the species as wild goat, Capra aegagrus, with the Bezoar ibex (C. a. aegagrus) as a subspecies. NatureServe lists Capra hircus as the domestic form of C. aegagrus and notes Grubb (1993, 2005) included C. aegagrus in C. hircus while Jones et al. (1992) kept them separate.

rangeSummary.value: Native from Turkey and the Caucasus east to Iran, Turkmenistan, Afghanistan and Pakistan. In North America, introduced to the Florida Mountains near Deming, New Mexico in 1970.

identification.text: About 30 in (76 cm) at the shoulder, hindquarters noticeably higher than the front on flat ground.
Mature males up to about 110 lb, females up to about 60 lb; both sexes grow horns (female horns average up to 15 in), male scimitar-shaped horns can exceed 50 in.

Light brown in summer; as the rut approaches mature males turn almost white ('white billies') with darkened leg markings, a black-brown cross over shoulders and back, dark face and jet-black beard and tail.
Compared with the feral goat: Wild goat is the ancestor of domestic goats; the sources read give no field mark separating the wild form from feral goats.

habitat.text: Steep, rocky terrain and cliffs (hooves are adapted to it); the New Mexico population lives in the Florida Mountains near Deming. Native habitat is forest, shrubland and rocky areas up to about 3,250 m in Turkey.

behavior.text: Hooves have a soft inner pocket ringed by a hard rim for clinging to rock; can jump several times their own height
Keen eyesight, notice movement more than half a mile away
Typically do not move much during the night
Seasonal breeding: females bear one to three young in early summer (Pakistan observations)

resources.title: Feral goat
resources.description: Identify the feral goat (Capra hircus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Feral goat (Capra hircus): Straight prominent horns (larger on males), rectangular pupils, coarse hair. Usually 25-55 kg, 1-1.2 m at the shoulder, 1-1.5 m long; males about 20% larger. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Feral populations occur on islands worldwide, including Hawaii and California's San Clemente Island; NatureServe records the species (Capra hircus) as present in Hawaii, New Mexico and California.

taxonomicNotes.text: That review lists synonyms Capra hircus aegagrus and Capra aegagrus hircus; NatureServe describes C. hircus as the domestic form of C. aegagrus.

rangeSummary.value: Feral populations occur on islands worldwide, including Hawaii and California's San Clemente Island; NatureServe records the species (Capra hircus) as present in Hawaii, New Mexico and California.

identification.text: Straight prominent horns (larger on males), rectangular pupils, coarse hair.
Usually 25-55 kg, 1-1.2 m at the shoulder, 1-1.5 m long; males about 20% larger.
All males and some females are bearded; short, upward-pointing tail distinguishes goats from sheep.
Coat usually black, but white, grey, brown, red or any combination occurs.
Compared with the feral sheep: Goats have short, upward-pointing tails, which sheep lack (Pacific Science review).
Compared with the persian ibex: Wild ancestor species; sources read give no field mark separating it from feral goats.

habitat.text: Rugged mountain country, rocky crags and alpine meadows; survive on a wide variety of forage with limited water.

behavior.text: Herds with a modal group size of two to four; up to 100 not uncommon, groups up to 200 recorded in Hawaii
Three herd types: all-male bachelor herds, mixed-sex groups, and females with young
Generalist herbivores taking grasses, forbs and browse
Excellent eyesight with a 320-340 degree field of view

resources.title: Mouflon
resources.description: Identify the mouflon (Ovis musimon), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Mouflon (Ovis musimon): European mouflon rams are fox red-brown in summer, usually with a whitish saddle patch; ewes are brownish; both sexes darker in winter. Rams carry helix-shaped horns up to 80 cm; ewes are hornless on Sardinia and small-horned on Corsica. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: European mouflon originate from Corsica and Sardinia. In North America DLNR lists mouflon sheep and mouflon-feral hybrid sheep on Hawaii Island and mouflon on Lanai; Wikipedia says it is kept on game ranches in Texas and has been introduced to Hawaii.

taxonomicNotes.text: Names used for the European mouflon in the pages read: Wikipedia 'Mouflon' says it was once thought a subspecies of the mouflon but is now considered a feral descendant of domestic sheep, Ovis aries musimon (true mouflon = Ovis gmelini, wild sheep of Cyprus, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Iran, Turkey; O. g. gmelini said to be introduced to Texas). Wikipedia 'European mouflon' is titled Ovis aries musimon and also mentions Ovis musimon, Ovis musimon musimon, Ovis ammon musimon and Ovis orientalis musimon. NatureServe (Ovis aries) says Grubb included O. orientalis, O. musimon and O. ophion in Ovis aries and that O. aries is the domestic form of O. gmelini. ADW's classification page is Ovis aries musimon and its Ovis aries page calls the Sardinia/Corsica flocks Ovis musimon. No 'Ovis gmelini musimon' appeared in any page read. Not resolved.
The European mouflon; authorities differ on whether it is a wild species or feral domestic sheep (Ovis aries musimon)

rangeSummary.value: European mouflon originate from Corsica and Sardinia. In North America DLNR lists mouflon sheep and mouflon-feral hybrid sheep on Hawaii Island and mouflon on Lanai; Wikipedia says it is kept on game ranches in Texas and has been introduced to Hawaii.

identification.text: European mouflon rams are fox red-brown in summer, usually with a whitish saddle patch; ewes are brownish; both sexes darker in winter.
Rams carry helix-shaped horns up to 80 cm; ewes are hornless on Sardinia and small-horned on Corsica.
Up to 120 cm body length, 90 cm shoulder height; rams 35-55 kg, ewes 25-40 kg.
Compared with the feral sheep: Hybrids with feral sheep are managed on Mauna Kea; the sources read give no field mark separating hybrids from mouflon.

habitat.text: Open, mountainous, stony dry ground originally; in Central Europe also deciduous and mixed forest, still preferring dry stony soils.

behavior.text: Small herds led by an older ewe; rams often form separate groups outside the rut
Rut in October/November; one or two lambs born March/April
Herbivores that debark trees
Escape behaviour is to flee to inaccessible rock faces; sight is well developed and people can be noticed at up to about 1,000 m

resources.title: Feral sheep
resources.description: Identify the feral sheep (Ovis aries), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Feral sheep (Ovis aries): Head-body 1,200-1,800 mm, shoulder 650-1,270 mm; ewes two-thirds to three-quarters the size of rams. Coloration from milky white to dark brown and black; wool, horns and external ears vary by breed. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Domestic sheep are established worldwide as introduced animals. DLNR lists feral sheep and mouflon-feral hybrid sheep on Hawaii Island (Mauna Kea); NatureServe records Ovis aries in Wyoming and Hawaii.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe: Ovis aries is the domestic form of O. gmelini; Grubb included O. orientalis, O. musimon and O. ophion (now feral) in O. aries.

rangeSummary.value: Domestic sheep are established worldwide as introduced animals. DLNR lists feral sheep and mouflon-feral hybrid sheep on Hawaii Island (Mauna Kea); NatureServe records Ovis aries in Wyoming and Hawaii.

identification.text: Head-body 1,200-1,800 mm, shoulder 650-1,270 mm; ewes two-thirds to three-quarters the size of rams.
Coloration from milky white to dark brown and black; wool, horns and external ears vary by breed.
Vertical cleft in a narrow, short-haired snout.
Domestic-derived; goats can be told from sheep by their short, upward-pointing tails (Pacific Science review of feral goats).
Compared with the mouflon: European mouflon has a reddish-brown summer coat with whitish saddle patch and rams' helix horns; hybrids with feral sheep occur on Mauna Kea.

habitat.text: Extremely versatile: desert, grassland, chaparral, forest and mountain.

behavior.text: Strong flocking instinct, groups up to 1,000 or more, with dominance hierarchies
Distressed when separated, often calling and pawing the ground
Grazers that alternate feeding and rumination

resources.title: Feral ferret
resources.description: Identify the feral ferret (Mustela furo), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Feral ferret (Mustela furo): Long slender body; adults 33-41 cm plus tail (males larger, 0.9-2.7 kg; females 0.3-1.1 kg). Three basic colour forms: dark polecat-type, sandy/pastel with brownish guard hairs, or all white; feral populations tend toward the wild polecat colour. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Domestic worldwide. The sources read document feral populations mainly outside North America (New Zealand, islands); CDFW discusses escapes and case studies in the US but does not describe an established North American feral population.

taxonomicNotes.text: Domesticated form of the European polecat; Animal Diversity Web, CDFW and the Global Invasive Species Database also write it M. putorius furo, and note unresolved taxonomy.

rangeSummary.value: Domestic worldwide. The sources read document feral populations mainly outside North America (New Zealand, islands); CDFW discusses escapes and case studies in the US but does not describe an established North American feral population.

identification.text: Long slender body; adults 33-41 cm plus tail (males larger, 0.9-2.7 kg; females 0.3-1.1 kg).
Three basic colour forms: dark polecat-type, sandy/pastel with brownish guard hairs, or all white; feral populations tend toward the wild polecat colour.
Five non-retractable claws on each paw; 34 teeth.
Compared with the black-footed ferret: A different, native North American species (Mustela nigripes); not a feral domestic ferret.

habitat.text: In New Zealand: grasslands, scrub, pasture, riverbeds, forest fringes and urban edges.

behavior.text: Crepuscular; sleeps 18-20 hours a day as a pet
Obligate carnivore of small prey; in New Zealand feral ferrets rely mainly on rabbits
Dens in rabbit holes, scrub, buildings and haystacks
Wild ferrets live about two to four years

resources.title: Alaska marmot
resources.description: Identify the alaska marmot (Marmota broweri), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Alaska marmot (Marmota broweri): Black fur on top of the head from nose to neck; coarse brown and black back. 21-26 in. long, 5.5-8.8 lb; males slightly larger than females. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Brooks Range of northern Alaska, perhaps also northern Yukon (unconfirmed).

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes it was previously treated as a synonym or subspecies of the hoary marmot (M. caligata).

rangeSummary.value: Brooks Range of northern Alaska, perhaps also northern Yukon (unconfirmed).

identification.text: Black fur on top of the head from nose to neck; coarse brown and black back.
21-26 in. long, 5.5-8.8 lb; males slightly larger than females.
Bushy tail; short muscular legs, small round eyes, broad rounded ears.

habitat.text: Boulder fields and talus slopes with large rocks next to productive tundra, about 3,250-4,000 ft.

behavior.text: Colonies of up to 50, each with its own den
Hibernates about late August to early June, waking every 3-4 weeks
Sentinel alarm calls vary by predator
Eats grasses, forbs, legumes and fruit near burrows

resources.title: Mountain beaver
resources.description: Identify the mountain beaver (Aplodontia rufa), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Mountain beaver (Aplodontia rufa): 300-500 mm body with only a 10-25 mm furred tail; about 800 g. Blackish, very coarse fur with a small white spot at the base of each ear. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southwestern British Columbia south along the Cascade, Olympic, Coast and Siskiyou ranges to central California and the Sierra Nevada.

taxonomicNotes.text: Listed only as unprotected where audited; unprotected status alone does not establish a hunting opportunity

rangeSummary.value: Southwestern British Columbia south along the Cascade, Olympic, Coast and Siskiyou ranges to central California and the Sierra Nevada.

identification.text: 300-500 mm body with only a 10-25 mm furred tail; about 800 g.
Blackish, very coarse fur with a small white spot at the base of each ear.
Thickset with a cylindrical body.

habitat.text: Damp ravines and shaded slopes in coastal and montane conifer forest with dense ground cover, often near watercourses.

behavior.text: Mostly fossorial and more active at night; tunnels along stream banks
Not aquatic or arboreal, though it swims and can climb
Eats ferns and other vegetation and stores haypiles for winter; active through the winter
Usually solitary, sometimes in loose colonies

conservationStatus.text: Point Arena mountain beaver (Aplodontia rufa nigra): listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Act since 1991-12-12.

resources.title: California ground squirrel
resources.description: Identify the california ground squirrel (Otospermophilus beecheyi), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: California ground squirrel (Otospermophilus beecheyi): Mottled gray, light and dark brown and white, with a darker mantle and lighter gray shoulders and neck. White ring around each eye. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: North-central California and west-central Nevada south to Baja California.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe (Phuong et al. 2014) splits the northern lineage as O. douglasii, narrowing O. beecheyi; Animal Diversity Web uses Spermophilus beecheyi and an older, wider range.
Listed only as unprotected where audited; unprotected status alone does not establish a hunting opportunity

rangeSummary.value: North-central California and west-central Nevada south to Baja California.

identification.text: Mottled gray, light and dark brown and white, with a darker mantle and lighter gray shoulders and neck.
White ring around each eye.
Bushy tail in the same mixed colours.
Compared with the douglas's ground squirrel: The northern lineage formerly included in this species, now treated by NatureServe as O. douglasii.

habitat.text: Open areas in many plant communities from fields and grasslands to mountains; avoids deserts.

behavior.text: Diurnal; sunbathes; stays close to its burrow
Lives in loose burrow colonies; most of a population may be yearlings
May hibernate or aestivate depending on climate; active all day in warm weather
Omnivorous, mostly green vegetation in spring and seeds, berries and nuts later; cheek pouches to carry food

resources.title: Sambar
resources.description: Identify the sambar (Rusa unicolor), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Sambar (Rusa unicolor): Large; males 185-260 kg, females about 162 kg. Coarse dark coat with lighter brown to creamy underparts. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Native from India to southeastern China and the Malay Peninsula. Introduced and established in California, Texas and Florida (and Australia and New Zealand). Not native to Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: Formerly Cervus unicolor; NatureServe notes Groves & Grubb (2011) place it in Cervus and that Rusa may not be monophyletic.

rangeSummary.value: Native from India to southeastern China and the Malay Peninsula. Introduced and established in California, Texas and Florida (and Australia and New Zealand). Not native to Canada.

identification.text: Large; males 185-260 kg, females about 162 kg.
Coarse dark coat with lighter brown to creamy underparts.
Males have a dense neck mane and antlers with three or four tines up to 100 cm.
Bushy tail white on the underside, raised as a signal.

habitat.text: Forested hillsides, swamp forest and open scrub, from sea level to about 3,700 m.

behavior.text: Mostly nocturnal; rests in dense cover by day
Solitary or in groups up to about 8 females
Browses at dusk and night on leaves, bark, berries and grass
Proficient swimmers

resources.title: Himalayan tahr
resources.description: Identify the himalayan tahr (Hemitragus jemlahicus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Himalayan tahr (Hemitragus jemlahicus): Males about 73 kg with a thick neck and shoulder ruff; females about 36 kg. Curved horns: males to 450 mm, females to 190 mm. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Native to the Himalaya from Kashmir through northern India to Nepal and Sikkim, and southern Tibet. Introduced in New Zealand, California and South Africa (NatureServe); Animal Diversity Web also lists New Mexico and Ontario.

rangeSummary.value: Native to the Himalaya from Kashmir through northern India to Nepal and Sikkim, and southern Tibet. Introduced in New Zealand, California and South Africa (NatureServe); Animal Diversity Web also lists New Mexico and Ontario.

identification.text: Males about 73 kg with a thick neck and shoulder ruff; females about 36 kg.
Curved horns: males to 450 mm, females to 190 mm.
Winter coat darker, summer coat lighter brown.
Young uniformly brown with black front legs.

habitat.text: Rugged, mostly wooded slopes and rocky ground at 750-5,000 m.

behavior.text: Herds of 2-23; males separate from females outside the breeding season
Most active at dawn and dusk; moves up and down slopes daily
Grazes alpine herbs and subalpine plants

resources.title: Golden-mantled ground squirrel
resources.description: Identify the golden-mantled ground squirrel (Callospermophilus lateralis), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Golden-mantled ground squirrel (Callospermophilus lateralis): Golden-red mantle covering the head and shoulders (brighter in males, duller and grayer in winter pelage). One white stripe bordered by two black stripes along each side of the body, like a chipmunk, but no facial stripes; instead a whitish eye ring. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Western North America from eastern British Columbia and western Alberta south through the western United States to California, Arizona and New Mexico, at roughly 1,220-3,965 m.

taxonomicNotes.text: Animal Diversity Web and older literature use Spermophilus lateralis; NatureServe and the BC Conservation Data Centre (since March 2012) use Callospermophilus lateralis after Helgen et al. (2009) split Spermophilus; NatureServe notes C. saturatus was formerly included.
Listed only as unprotected where audited (Montana); unprotected status alone does not establish a hunting opportunity

rangeSummary.value: Western North America from eastern British Columbia and western Alberta south through the western United States to California, Arizona and New Mexico, at roughly 1,220-3,965 m.

identification.text: Golden-red mantle covering the head and shoulders (brighter in males, duller and grayer in winter pelage).
One white stripe bordered by two black stripes along each side of the body, like a chipmunk, but no facial stripes; instead a whitish eye ring.
Back gray, brownish or buff; underside whitish or yellowish-gray; tail brownish-black above and reddish-brown below.
Weighs roughly 120-394 g and is about 235-295 mm long.
Compared with the chipmunks (tamias spp.): Chipmunks have a white stripe through the eye; the golden-mantled ground squirrel has no facial striping and a golden-red head and mantle.
Compared with the cascade golden-mantled ground squirrel (callospermophilus saturatus): Formerly included in this species (NatureServe); the sources read give no field character to separate them.

habitat.text: Mountain slopes and foothills, alpine tundra, chaparral, open pine, spruce and fir forest, rocky outcrops and slides, meadow margins and rocky sagebrush country, reaching greatest abundance in open forest lacking dense understory; needs logs, stumps or rocks for cover, and is often at campgrounds.

behavior.text: Diurnal, active mainly March-November at low elevations with a shorter season in snowy high mountains; hibernates roughly October to April.
Asocial: females defend a burrow and surrounding area; burrows are under rocks, stumps, logs, trees, bushes or cabins, or in rock crevices or banks.
Omnivore eating seeds, fungus (about 65% of summer food in one study), leaves, flowers, fruits, roots, insects and carrion; carries food in cheek pouches and caches it.
Forages on the ground and in logs, stumps and shrubby vegetation.

resources.title: Appalachian cottontail
resources.description: Identify the appalachian cottontail (Sylvilagus obscurus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Appalachian cottontail (Sylvilagus obscurus): Yellowish brown mixed with black above, reddish-brown patch over the neck, lighter sides and white underside; short tail dark above and white beneath; 38.6-43.0 cm long, 0.8-1.0 kg. Compared with the eastern cottontail: slightly smaller, shorter rounded ears with black edging, a black spot between the ears and no white forehead spot. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Appalachian Mountains from the Hudson River in New York to northern Alabama; NatureServe lists Pennsylvania, Maryland, Virginia, West Virginia, Kentucky, Tennessee, North and South Carolina, Georgia and Alabama. Not recorded for Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes that S. obscurus is regarded by some as a junior synonym of S. transitionalis (New England cottontail).

rangeSummary.value: Appalachian Mountains from the Hudson River in New York to northern Alabama; NatureServe lists Pennsylvania, Maryland, Virginia, West Virginia, Kentucky, Tennessee, North and South Carolina, Georgia and Alabama. Not recorded for Canada.

identification.text: Yellowish brown mixed with black above, reddish-brown patch over the neck, lighter sides and white underside; short tail dark above and white beneath; 38.6-43.0 cm long, 0.8-1.0 kg.
Compared with the eastern cottontail: slightly smaller, shorter rounded ears with black edging, a black spot between the ears and no white forehead spot.
Nearly indistinguishable from the New England cottontail in the field; distinguished by range (Appalachian is south or west of the Hudson River in New York) or skull.
Compared with the new england cottontail: Nearly indistinguishable in the field; range differs, with Appalachian south or west of the Hudson River in New York.
Compared with the eastern cottontail: Eastern is slightly larger with longer ears, usually a white forehead spot, and lacks the black spot between the ears.

habitat.text: High-elevation (generally above about 760 m) conifer forest and dense shrub cover such as mountain laurel, rhododendron, blueberry and blackberry; also young clearcuts. Nests are ground depressions lined with grass and fur.

behavior.text: Crepuscular, resting by day in cover such as under a log; active year-round and solitary, with male dominance hierarchies.
Diet: grasses, forbs and conifer needles, leaves, twigs and fruits; winter diet is mostly twigs, bark and buds (85% in Maryland and West Virginia) or evergreen needles in snow.
Home range up to 13.3 ha for breeding males and as little as 1.5 ha for females; litters of 3-5, occasionally 8.

resources.title: Antelope jackrabbit
resources.description: Identify the antelope jackrabbit (Lepus alleni), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Antelope jackrabbit (Lepus alleni): Very large jackrabbit with especially large head and tall ears (average 162 mm), mostly bare apart from white fringes on edges and tips. Flanks, limbs, hips and rump white with black tips; belly, chin, throat and tail white. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern Arizona through western Mexico to northern Nayarit, and Tiburon Island; sea level to about 1,500 m in Arizona.

rangeSummary.value: Southern Arizona through western Mexico to northern Nayarit, and Tiburon Island; sea level to about 1,500 m in Arizona.

identification.text: Very large jackrabbit with especially large head and tall ears (average 162 mm), mostly bare apart from white fringes on edges and tips.
Flanks, limbs, hips and rump white with black tips; belly, chin, throat and tail white.
Upper body yellow-brown with some black.

habitat.text: Arid grassy areas with scattered large shrubs, desert with little grass, foothills, mesas and bajadas; less common in barren desert and valley-bottom mesquite.

behavior.text: Primarily nocturnal and crepuscular, also active in the morning; rests in shade by day in forms under grass, brush, cactus or mesquite.
May travel up to about a mile between daytime cover and nocturnal feeding area; fast runner with great leaping ability.
Eats grasses, mesquite, cacti and other desert plants; relies on mesquite leaves and cacti in the dry season and grass in the wet season.
NatureServe says it may form groups up to 25; Animal Diversity Web calls it solitary.

content.plainText: Confirm a american ermine before you act. Compared with the beringian ermine: Same look; Alaska and western Yukon to Arctic Canada animals are M. erminea per NatureServe.
Confirm a ermine before you act. Compared with the american ermine: Same appearance; separated by range, with M. richardsonii across most of Canada and the northern US.
Confirm a long-tailed weasel before you act. Compared with the least weasel: Far smaller with a short tail and no black tip in winter.
Confirm a least weasel before you act. Compared with the ermine / stoat: Larger with a black tail tip in winter.
Confirm a western spotted skunk before you act. Compared with the eastern spotted skunk: Looks similar but with less extensive white.
Confirm a eastern spotted skunk before you act. Compared with the western spotted skunk: White areas more extensive on the western species.
Confirm a ringtail before you act. Compared with the raccoon: ADW notes a ringed tail much like a raccoon's; ringtail is far slimmer, cat-like, with a much longer tail.
Confirm a swift fox before you act. Compared with the kit fox: Larger ears, narrower snout, longer tail; more arid southwestern range.
Confirm a kit fox before you act. Compared with the swift fox: Smaller ears, broader snout, shorter tail; Great Plains range.
Confirm a pacific marten before you act. Compared with the american marten: Separate species; Alaska, British Columbia, Idaho and Montana have both. NatureServe cites Dawson and Cook (2012).
Confirm a white-nosed coati before you act. Compared with the ringtail: Much smaller, cat-like, with a short muzzle and a black-and-white ringed tail.
Confirm a white-tailed prairie dog before you act. Compared with the black-tailed prairie dog: Black-tipped tail and a lower-elevation, grassland habitat.
Confirm a gunnison's prairie dog before you act. Compared with the white-tailed prairie dog: Pure white distal tail hairs versus grayish-white on Gunnison's.
Confirm a yellow-bellied marmot before you act. Compared with the hoary marmot: Black feet, black cap and white nose patch.
Confirm a hoary marmot before you act. Compared with the yellow-bellied marmot: Lacks black feet and white nose patch; frosted tawny coat.
Confirm a douglas squirrel before you act. Compared with the red squirrel: Lacks the orange chest and belly of Douglas squirrel (ADW).
Confirm a northern flying squirrel before you act. Compared with the southern flying squirrel: Smaller, with cream-coloured rather than grey-based belly fur.
Confirm a southern flying squirrel before you act. Compared with the northern flying squirrel: Larger, with grey-based belly hairs rather than cream.
Confirm a alaska hare before you act. Compared with the arctic hare: Very similar; separated mainly by range (source says they occupy different geographic ranges).
Confirm a european rabbit before you act. Compared with the european hare: Hares have longer ears and legs and do not live in warrens.
Confirm a marsh rabbit before you act. Compared with the eastern cottontail: Larger head and tail; tail underside white.
Confirm a collared pika before you act. Compared with the american pika: Lacks the collar and buff facial-gland patch (source says differs mainly in fur colouration).
Confirm a red deer before you act. Compared with the white-tailed deer: Occupies similar habitat but is much smaller (source only notes association).
Confirm a persian ibex before you act. Compared with the feral goat: Wild goat is the ancestor of domestic goats; the sources read give no field mark separating the wild form from feral goats.
Confirm a feral goat before you act. Compared with the feral sheep: Goats have short, upward-pointing tails, which sheep lack (Pacific Science review).
Confirm a mouflon before you act. Compared with the feral sheep: Hybrids with feral sheep are managed on Mauna Kea; the sources read give no field mark separating hybrids from mouflon.

Confirm a feral sheep before you act. Compared with the mouflon: European mouflon has a reddish-brown summer coat with whitish saddle patch and rams' helix horns; hybrids with feral sheep occur on Mauna Kea.
Confirm a feral ferret before you act. Compared with the black-footed ferret: A different, native North American species (Mustela nigripes); not a feral domestic ferret.
Confirm a california ground squirrel before you act. Compared with the douglas's ground squirrel: The northern lineage formerly included in this species, now treated by NatureServe as O. douglasii.

Confirm a golden-mantled ground squirrel before you act. Compared with the chipmunks (tamias spp.): Chipmunks have a white stripe through the eye; the golden-mantled ground squirrel has no facial striping and a golden-red head and mantle.

Confirm a appalachian cottontail before you act. Compared with the new england cottontail: Nearly indistinguishable in the field; range differs, with Appalachian south or west of the Hudson River in New York.
